items.stem: What is the relative charge of a proton?
items.markingKey: Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1.

items.stem: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
items.answer: It has equal numbers of protons (+1 each) and electrons (−1 each), so the charges cancel.
items.markingKey: equal numbers of protons and electrons [1]; charges cancel [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why some alpha particles were deflected through large angles in Rutherford’s experiment.
items.answer: Alpha particles are positive; those passing very close to the small positive nucleus were strongly repelled.
items.markingKey: alpha particles and nucleus both positive [1]; repelled when passing close [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom of nitrogen (N) has atomic number 7 and mass number 14. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the atom.
items.answer: 7 protons, 7 neutrons, 7 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = electrons = 7 [1]; neutrons = 14 − 7 = 7 [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom of potassium has atomic number 19 and mass number 39. (a) Calculate the number of neutrons. (b) Give the number of electrons and their arrangement in shells.
items.answer: (a) 20 (b) 19 electrons arranged 2,8,8,1

items.stem: Atom X has atomic number 8 and mass number 16; atom Y has atomic number 12 and mass number 24. (a) Calculate the number of neutrons in each atom. (b) Give the electron arrangement of each atom. (c) Deduce, with a reason, the group of the Periodic Table for each element.
items.answer: (a) X 8, Y 12 (b) X 2,6, Y 2,8,2 (c) X Group 6, Y Group 2, from the number of outer-shell electrons (full outer shell = Group 0).
items.markingKey: (a) 16 − 8 = 8 and 24 − 12 = 12 [1] (b) 2,6 and 2,8,2 [1] (c) groups from outer electrons [1]; both groups correct [1] [4]

items.stem: A computer simulation of the gold foil experiment fires 40000 alpha particles at gold atoms: 39794 go straight through, 200 are slightly deflected and 6 are reflected back. (a) Calculate the percentage of alpha particles that passed straight through. (b) Explain what the particles that bounced back show about the nucleus.
items.answer: (a) 99.49% (b) The nucleus is very small (few hits), dense/massive and positively charged (repels the positive alpha particles).
items.markingKey: (a) 39794 ÷ 40000 × 100 [1] = 99.49% [1] [2] (b) small [1]; positive / dense, repels alpha particles [1] [2]

items.stem: In a repeat of Rutherford’s experiment, 20000 alpha particles are fired at a thin gold foil. 19921 pass straight through, 75 are deflected through small angles and 4 bounce back. (a) Explain what the particles that bounced back show about the nucleus. (b) Suggest why the experiment uses a very thin foil. (c) State the charge on an alpha particle.
items.answer: (a) The nucleus is very small (few hits), dense/massive and positively charged (repels the positive alpha particles). (b) So that each alpha particle meets only a few layers of atoms and is not absorbed; deflections from single nuclei can be seen. (c) Positive (+2).
items.markingKey: (a) small [1]; positive / dense, repels alpha particles [1] [2] (b) avoid absorption / few atoms in the way [1]; single deflections observed [1] [2] (c) Positive (+2) [1]

items.stem: Which particle has a relative charge of 0?
items.answer: Neutron
items.markingKey: Neutrons are neutral.

items.stem: Where is most of the mass of an atom found?
options: In the empty space around the nucleus
items.answer: In the nucleus
items.markingKey: Protons and neutrons (mass 1 each) are in the nucleus; electrons have almost no mass.

items.stem: Describe the plum pudding model and explain how it differs from the nuclear model.
items.answer: Plum pudding: a ball of positive charge with electrons scattered through it. Nuclear model: positive charge and most mass in a tiny central nucleus, electrons around it, mostly empty space.
items.markingKey: plum pudding described [1]; nucleus small, dense, positive [1]; mostly empty space [1] [3]

items.stem: In a test, Zara writes: "The mass number tells you the number of neutrons." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: Mass number = protons + neutrons; neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
items.markingKey: mass number definition [1]; neutrons = A − Z [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom has 13 protons and 14 neutrons. Identify the element and state its mass number.
items.answer: Aluminium; mass number 27
items.markingKey: aluminium (from 13 protons) [1]; mass number = 13 + 14 = 27 [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom has 15 protons and 16 neutrons. (a) Identify the element. (b) State its mass number. (c) Draw or describe the arrangement of electrons in the atom.
items.answer: (a) Phosphorus (b) 31 (c) 15 electrons: 2,8,5

items.stem: In a repeat of Rutherford’s experiment, 20000 alpha particles are fired at a thin gold foil. 19792 pass straight through, 200 are deflected through small angles and 8 bounce back. (a) Calculate the percentage of alpha particles that passed straight through. (b) Explain what the particles that bounced back show about the nucleus. (c) Suggest why the experiment uses a very thin foil.
items.answer: (a) 98.96% (b) The nucleus is very small (few hits), dense/massive and positively charged (repels the positive alpha particles). (c) So that each alpha particle meets only a few layers of atoms and is not absorbed; deflections from single nuclei can be seen.
items.markingKey: (a) 19792 ÷ 20000 × 100 [1] = 98.96% [1] [2] (b) small [1]; positive / dense, repels alpha particles [1] [2] (c) avoid absorption / few atoms in the way [1]; single deflections observed [1] [2]

items.stem: What name is given to the elements in Group 1?
items.answer: Alkali metals
items.markingKey: Group 1 metals react with water to form alkaline solutions.

items.stem: Explain why sodium and potassium are stored under oil.
items.answer: They react quickly with oxygen and water vapour in the air; oil keeps air and water away.
items.markingKey: react with air / water [1]; oil excludes air and water [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why helium is used to fill party balloons and airships.
items.answer: It is much less dense than air, so the balloon floats, and it is unreactive, so it will not burn (unlike hydrogen).
items.markingKey: low density [1]; unreactive / non-flammable [1] [2]

items.stem: The boiling points of some noble gases are: helium −269 °C, neon −246 °C, argon −186 °C, krypton −153 °C, xenon ?, radon −62 °C. Describe the trend in boiling point down the group and estimate the boiling point of xenon.
items.answer: The boiling point increases down the group; estimate between −153 and −62 °C (actual −108 °C).
items.markingKey: increases down the group [1]; value between −153 and −62 °C [1] [2]

items.stem: The boiling points of some noble gases are: helium −269 °C, neon −246 °C, argon −186 °C, krypton ?, xenon −108 °C, radon −62 °C. (a) Estimate the missing value. (b) Explain why the noble gases are all used where an unreactive gas is needed.
items.answer: (a) between −186 and −108 °C (actual −153 °C) (b) Their atoms have full outer shells, so they do not form compounds easily.
items.markingKey: (a) in range [1] (b) full outer shells [1]; do not react [1] [3]

items.stem: In a demonstration in Santiago, a teacher drops a rice-grain-sized piece of lithium into water, then repeats with sodium. Universal indicator is in the water. (a) Predict which metal reacts more vigorously and explain why. (b) State and explain the final colour of the universal indicator.
items.answer: (a) Sodium: it is lower in Group 1; its outer electron is further from the nucleus and is lost more easily. (b) Purple (or blue): the metal hydroxide formed is an alkali.
items.markingKey: (a) sodium [1]; outer electron further / lost more easily [1] [2] (b) purple / blue [1]; alkali formed [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why argon is used inside filament lamps.
items.answer: Argon is unreactive, so the hot filament does not react with it (it would burn in oxygen).
items.markingKey: unreactive [1]; filament does not react / burn [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why potassium reacts more vigorously with water than lithium.
items.answer: Potassium’s outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily; potassium is more reactive.
items.markingKey: outer electron further from nucleus [1]; lost more easily [1] [2]

items.stem: The boiling points of some noble gases are: helium −269 °C, neon −246 °C, argon ?, krypton −153 °C, xenon −108 °C, radon −62 °C. Describe the trend in boiling point down the group and estimate the boiling point of argon.
items.answer: The boiling point increases down the group; estimate between −246 and −153 °C (actual −186 °C).
items.markingKey: increases down the group [1]; value between −246 and −153 °C [1] [2]

items.stem: Kwame watches a teacher add small pieces of sodium and potassium to separate troughs of water containing universal indicator. (a) Describe a test for the gas given off. (b) Explain why caesium is not used in school demonstrations.
items.answer: (a) Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of a test tube of the gas: it burns with a squeaky pop (hydrogen). (b) Caesium is even further down Group 1 so it reacts explosively with water.
items.markingKey: (a) lighted splint [1]; squeaky pop [1] [2] (b) more reactive down group [1]; explosive / dangerous [1] [2]

items.stem: Chloe watches a teacher add small pieces of lithium and sodium to separate troughs of water containing universal indicator. (a) Give two safety precautions the teacher should take. (b) Explain why caesium is not used in school demonstrations.
items.answer: (a) Use only a tiny piece; use safety screen and eye protection; handle with tongs, not fingers. (b) Caesium is even further down Group 1 so it reacts explosively with water.
items.markingKey: (a) any two [1] each [2] (b) more reactive down group [1]; explosive / dangerous [1] [2]

items.stem: What is an ionic bond?
options: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
The attraction between oppositely charged ions
A bond between two noble gas atoms
items.answer: The attraction between oppositely charged ions
items.markingKey: Ionic bond: electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions formed by electron transfer.

items.stem: Explain why a sodium ion has a charge of 1+.
items.answer: It has 11 protons but only 10 electrons after losing one electron, so there is one more positive charge than negative.
items.markingKey: 11 protons, 10 electrons [1]; one extra positive charge [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why noble gas atoms do not usually form bonds.
items.answer: They already have full outer shells, so they do not need to gain, lose or share electrons.
items.markingKey: full outer shell [1]; no need to gain/lose/share [1] [2]

items.stem: Magnesium (atomic number 12) reacts with chlorine (atomic number 17) to form magnesium chloride. State how many electrons each metal atom loses and give the charges on the two ions.
items.answer: 2 electrons lost; Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻
items.markingKey: 2 lost [1]; ions Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ [1] [2]

items.stem: Magnesium (atomic number 12) reacts with fluorine (atomic number 9) to form magnesium fluoride. (a) Give the electron arrangements of both atoms. (b) Describe what happens to the electrons when they react. (c) Deduce the formula of the compound.
items.answer: (a) magnesium 2,8,2; fluorine 2,7 (b) each magnesium atom loses 2 electrons and each fluorine atom gains 1, forming Mg²⁺ and F⁻ (c) MgF₂
items.markingKey: (a) both arrangements [1] (b) transfer described with charges [1] (c) MgF₂ [1] [3]

items.stem: Calcium (atomic number 20) reacts with chlorine (atomic number 17) to form calcium chloride. (a) Give the electron arrangements of the atoms and of the ions formed. (b) Explain how the ions are held together. (c) Deduce the formula, showing how the charges balance.
items.answer: (a) calcium 2,8,8,2 → Ca²⁺ 2,8,8; chlorine 2,8,7 → Cl⁻ 2,8,8 (b) strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (ionic bonds) (c) 1 × (2+) = 2 × (1−), so CaCl₂
items.markingKey: (a) atoms [1]; ions with full outer shells [1] (b) attraction between opposite ions [1] (c) CaCl₂ with charge balance [1] [4]

items.stem: Freya is given three mystery elements: X (atomic number 19), Y (atomic number 17) and Z (atomic number 7). (a) Give the electron arrangement of each element. (b) State which element is a metal and explain how you know.
items.answer: (a) X 2,8,8,1; Y 2,8,7; Z 2,5 (b) X: it has 1 outer electron, which it loses easily (Group 1).
items.markingKey: (a) all three correct [2]; two correct [1] [2] (b) X [1]; few outer electrons / Group 1 [1] [2]

items.stem: Element X has atomic number 12, element Y has atomic number 9 and element Z has atomic number 7. (a) Describe how X and Y bond together and give the formula of the compound. (b) Explain why neither X nor Y forms a bond with argon.
items.answer: (a) X loses 2 electrons to form X²⁺; Y gains 1 to form Y⁻; ionic bonding; formula XY₂. (b) Argon has a full outer shell (2,8,8), so it does not gain, lose or share electrons.
items.markingKey: (a) electron transfer with charges [1]; ionic attraction [1]; XY₂ [1] [3] (b) full outer shell [1]; no electron transfer or sharing [1] [2]

items.stem: What is a covalent bond?
options: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
The transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal
The attraction between oppositely charged ions
The attraction between protons and neutrons
items.answer: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
items.markingKey: Covalent: non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons.

items.stem: Ionic bonding usually happens between …
items.answer: a metal and a non-metal
items.markingKey: Metals lose electrons; non-metals gain them.

items.stem: Explain why magnesium oxide has the formula MgO.
items.answer: Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺ and oxygen gains two to form O²⁻; one of each balances the charges.
items.markingKey: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ [1]; charges balance 1:1 [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the formula of potassium sulfide?
items.answer: K₂S
items.markingKey: K⁺ and S²⁻: charges balance in K₂S.

items.stem: Nitrogen (atomic number 7) forms a covalent compound with hydrogen. State the number of electrons in the outer shell of a nitrogen atom and deduce the formula of the compound.
items.answer: 5 outer electrons; NH₃
items.markingKey: 5 [1]; NH₃ (3 shared pairs) [1] [2]

items.stem: Nitrogen (atomic number 7) forms a covalent compound with hydrogen. (a) Give the electron arrangement of nitrogen. (b) Explain how many hydrogen atoms bond to each nitrogen atom. (c) Name the compound and give its formula.
items.answer: (a) 2,5 (b) 3: it needs 3 more electrons for a full outer shell and shares one pair with each hydrogen (c) ammonia, NH₃
items.markingKey: (a) 2,5 [1] (b) 3 with reason [1] (c) name and formula [1] [3]

items.stem: Which substance has a giant covalent structure?
items.answer: Diamond
items.markingKey: Diamond: each carbon atom covalently bonded to four others in a giant structure.

items.stem: Explain why diamond is very hard.
items.answer: Each carbon atom is joined to four others by strong covalent bonds in a giant 3-D structure, so a lot of force is needed to break it.
items.markingKey: four strong covalent bonds per atom [1]; giant rigid structure [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why graphite is soft and slippery and is used in pencils.
items.answer: It is made of layers of carbon atoms with weak forces between the layers, so the layers slide over each other and rub off onto paper.
items.markingKey: layers [1]; weak forces between layers so they slide [1] [2]

items.stem: Tariq tests three unknown substances. P: melting point 1610 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; Q: melting point −218 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; R: melting point 858 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes. Identify the structure of substance Q and give a reason.
items.answer: Simple molecular: low melting point (weak forces between molecules) and does not conduct.
items.markingKey: simple molecular [1]; reason from data [1] [2]

items.stem: Mei tests three unknown substances. P: melting point 680 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; Q: melting point 1610 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; R: melting point −78 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no. Identify the type of structure of each substance.
items.answer: P: giant ionic. Q: giant covalent. R: simple molecular.
items.markingKey: one mark each for P, Q and R [3]

items.stem: An engineering company in Istanbul uses silicon dioxide (sand) for making glass and graphite for electrodes in electrolysis. (a) Explain why silicon dioxide (sand) is suitable for making glass. (b) Explain why graphite is suitable for electrodes in electrolysis.
items.answer: (a) It has a giant covalent structure and a high melting point, so glass is hard and heat-resistant. (b) It conducts electricity and has a very high melting point.
items.markingKey: (a) property [1]; linked to structure [1] [2] (b) property [1]; linked to structure [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does.
items.answer: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions; when molten they are free to move and carry charge.
items.markingKey: ions fixed in solid [1]; free to move when molten [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why water boils at a much lower temperature than sand (silicon dioxide).
items.answer: Water is simple molecular with weak forces between molecules; sand is giant covalent, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken.
items.markingKey: water weak forces between molecules [1]; sand giant covalent strong bonds [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf tests three unknown substances. P: melting point 996 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; Q: melting point 1410 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; R: melting point −182 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no. Identify the structure of substance P and give a reason.
items.answer: Giant ionic: high melting point and conducts only when molten (ions free to move).
items.markingKey: giant ionic [1]; reason from data [1] [2]

items.stem: An engineering company in Accra uses diamond for the tips of drill bits and silicon dioxide (sand) for making glass. (a) Explain why diamond is suitable for the tips of drill bits. (b) Explain why a simple molecular substance such as wax would be unsuitable for this work. (c) Suggest one property, other than melting point, that should be tested before choosing a material.
items.answer: (a) It is the hardest substance (strong covalent bonds in a giant structure). (b) It has a low melting point and is soft, because only weak forces act between its molecules. (c) Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches.
items.markingKey: (a) property [1]; linked to structure [1] [2] (b) low melting point / soft [1]; weak forces between molecules [1] [2] (c) valid property with reason [1]; Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches [1] [2]

items.stem: In Rutherford’s gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What did this show?
options: The nucleus fills most of the atom
The atom is a solid ball of positive charge
Most of the atom is empty space
items.answer: Most of the atom is empty space
items.markingKey: Particles passed through without hitting anything, so the atom is mostly empty space.

items.stem: Explain how atoms of two different elements differ.
items.answer: They have different numbers of protons (different atomic numbers), and so different numbers of electrons.
items.markingKey: different number of protons [1]; so different atomic number / electrons [1] [2]

items.stem: Kwame says: "The mass number tells you the number of neutrons." Explain why Kwame is wrong.
items.answer: Mass number = protons + neutrons; neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
items.markingKey: mass number definition [1]; neutrons = A − Z [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom of calcium (Ca) has atomic number 20 and mass number 40. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the atom.
items.answer: 20 protons, 20 neutrons, 20 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = electrons = 20 [1]; neutrons = 40 − 20 = 20 [1] [2]

items.stem: In a repeat of Rutherford’s experiment, 20000 alpha particles are fired at a thin gold foil. 19848 pass straight through, 150 are deflected through small angles and 2 bounce back. (a) Calculate the percentage of alpha particles that passed straight through. (b) Explain what the particles that passed straight through show about atoms.
items.answer: (a) 99.24% (b) Most of the atom is empty space.
items.markingKey: (a) 19848 ÷ 20000 × 100 [1] = 99.24% [1] [2] (b) Most of the atom is empty space [1]

items.stem: What name is given to the elements in Group 7?
items.answer: Halogens
items.markingKey: Group 7: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine.

items.stem: Explain why the solution formed when lithium reacts with water turns universal indicator purple.
items.answer: Lithium hydroxide is formed, which is an alkali, so the solution has a high pH.
items.markingKey: lithium hydroxide formed [1]; alkaline / high pH [1] [2]

items.stem: The boiling points of some noble gases are: helium −269 °C, neon −246 °C, argon −186 °C, krypton ?, xenon −108 °C, radon −62 °C. Describe the trend in boiling point down the group and estimate the boiling point of krypton.
items.answer: The boiling point increases down the group; estimate between −186 and −108 °C (actual −153 °C).
items.markingKey: increases down the group [1]; value between −186 and −108 °C [1] [2]

items.stem: In a demonstration in Singapore, a teacher drops a rice-grain-sized piece of sodium into water, then repeats with potassium. Universal indicator is in the water. (a) Describe a test for the gas given off. (b) Give two safety precautions the teacher should take.
items.answer: (a) Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of a test tube of the gas: it burns with a squeaky pop (hydrogen). (b) Use only a tiny piece; use safety screen and eye protection; handle with tongs, not fingers.
items.markingKey: (a) lighted splint [1]; squeaky pop [1] [2] (b) any two [1] each [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the charge on a chloride ion? (b) What is an ionic bond?
items.answer: (a) 1− (b) The attraction between oppositely charged ions
items.markingKey: (a) Cl (2,8,7) gains one electron to give Cl⁻ (2,8,8). (b) Ionic bond: electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions formed by electron transfer.

items.stem: Describe the difference between ionic and covalent bonding.
items.answer: Ionic: electrons are transferred from a metal to a non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions that attract. Covalent: non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons.
items.markingKey: ionic = transfer and ions attract [1]; covalent = sharing pairs [1] [2]

items.stem: Sodium (atomic number 11) reacts with sulfur (atomic number 16) to form sodium sulfide. State how many electrons each metal atom loses and give the charges on the two ions.
items.answer: 1 electron lost; Na⁺ and S²⁻
items.markingKey: 1 lost [1]; ions Na⁺ and S²⁻ [1] [2]

items.stem: Chlorine (atomic number 17) forms a covalent compound with hydrogen. State the number of electrons in the outer shell of a chlorine atom and deduce the formula of the compound.
items.answer: 7 outer electrons; ClH
items.markingKey: 7 [1]; ClH (1 shared pairs) [1] [2]

items.stem: Sodium (atomic number 11) reacts with fluorine (atomic number 9) to form sodium fluoride. (a) Give the electron arrangements of both atoms. (b) Describe what happens to the electrons when they react. (c) Deduce the formula of the compound.
items.answer: (a) sodium 2,8,1; fluorine 2,7 (b) each sodium atom loses 1 electron and each fluorine atom gains 1, forming Na⁺ and F⁻ (c) NaF
items.markingKey: (a) both arrangements [1] (b) transfer described with charges [1] (c) NaF [1] [3]

items.stem: Element X has atomic number 11, element Y has atomic number 16 and element Z has atomic number 6. (a) Give the electron arrangement of each element. (b) State which element is a metal and explain how you know. (c) Explain why neither X nor Y forms a bond with argon.
items.answer: (a) X 2,8,1; Y 2,8,6; Z 2,4 (b) X: it has 1 outer electron, which it loses easily (Group 1). (c) Argon has a full outer shell (2,8,8), so it does not gain, lose or share electrons.
items.markingKey: (a) all three correct [2]; two correct [1] [2] (b) X [1]; few outer electrons / Group 1 [1] [2] (c) full outer shell [1]; no electron transfer or sharing [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
items.answer: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one electron per atom free to move; in diamond all four outer electrons are used in bonds.
items.markingKey: graphite: free (delocalised) electrons [1]; diamond: all electrons in bonds [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why iodine turns to a gas at a low temperature even though the atoms in an iodine molecule are joined by a covalent bond.
items.answer: Only the weak forces between I₂ molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break.
items.markingKey: weak forces between molecules overcome [1]; covalent bond not broken [1] [2]

items.stem: Mohammed tests three unknown substances. P: melting point 2072 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; Q: melting point 680 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; R: melting point −218 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no. items.answer: Giant ionic: high melting point and conducts only when molten (ions free to move).
items.markingKey: giant ionic [1]; reason from data [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel reads that magnesium oxide is used for lining furnaces, while graphite is used for a lubricant in machinery. (a) Explain why magnesium oxide is suitable for lining furnaces. (b) Suggest one property, other than melting point, that should be tested before choosing a material.
items.answer: (a) It has a very high melting point (giant ionic). (b) Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches.
items.markingKey: (a) property [1]; linked to structure [1] [2] (b) valid property with reason [1]; Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches [1] [2]

Electrons are spread evenly through the atom
items.answer: The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
items.markingKey: Only a small, massive, positive centre could repel alpha particles straight back.

items.stem: Explain why scientists accepted Rutherford’s model in place of the plum pudding model.
items.answer: It explained all the results, including the large deflections that the plum pudding model could not, and other scientists could repeat the experiment.
items.markingKey: explains the deflections [1]; repeatable evidence [1] [2]

items.stem: Lina says: "The mass number tells you the number of neutrons." Explain why Lina is wrong.
items.answer: Mass number = protons + neutrons; neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
items.markingKey: mass number definition [1]; neutrons = A − Z [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom has 20 protons and 20 neutrons. Identify the element and state its mass number.
items.answer: Calcium; mass number 40
items.markingKey: calcium (from 20 protons) [1]; mass number = 20 + 20 = 40 [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom of boron has atomic number 5 and mass number 11. (a) Calculate the number of neutrons. (b) Give the number of electrons and their arrangement in shells.
items.answer: (a) 6 (b) 5 electrons arranged 2,3
items.markingKey: (a) 11 − 5 = 6 [1] (b) 5 electrons [1]; arrangement 2,3 [1] [3]

items.stem: In a repeat of Rutherford’s experiment, 50000 alpha particles are fired at a thin gold foil. 49846 pass straight through, 150 are deflected through small angles and 4 bounce back. (a) Explain why the plum pudding model cannot explain these results. (b) Suggest why the experiment uses a very thin foil. (c) State the charge on an alpha particle.
items.answer: (a) In that model positive charge is spread out thinly, so it could not deflect alpha particles strongly or turn them back. (b) So that each alpha particle meets only a few layers of atoms and is not absorbed; deflections from single nuclei can be seen. (c) Positive (+2).
items.markingKey: (a) positive charge spread out [1]; could not cause large deflection / bounce back [1] [2] (b) avoid absorption / few atoms in the way [1]; single deflections observed [1] [2] (c) Positive (+2) [1]

items.stem: Why are the noble gases very unreactive?
options: Their atoms have full outer electron shells
Their atoms have one outer electron
items.answer: Their atoms have full outer electron shells
items.markingKey: A full outer shell is stable, so they do not need to gain, lose or share electrons.

items.stem: Describe what you would see when a small piece of sodium is placed on water.
items.answer: It floats, melts into a silvery ball, fizzes and moves around on the surface, getting smaller until it disappears.
items.markingKey: floats / melts into ball [1]; fizzes / moves / disappears [1] [2]

items.stem: The boiling points of some Group 7 elements are: fluorine −188 °C, chlorine ?, bromine 59 °C, iodine 184 °C. Describe the trend in boiling point down the group and estimate the boiling point of chlorine.
items.answer: The boiling point increases down the group; estimate between −188 and 59 °C (actual −34 °C).
items.markingKey: increases down the group [1]; value between −188 and 59 °C [1] [2]

items.stem: In a demonstration in Santiago, a teacher drops a rice-grain-sized piece of lithium into water, then repeats with sodium. Universal indicator is in the water. (a) Predict which metal reacts more vigorously and explain why. (b) Give two safety precautions the teacher should take.
items.answer: (a) Sodium: it is lower in Group 1; its outer electron is further from the nucleus and is lost more easily. (b) Use only a tiny piece; use safety screen and eye protection; handle with tongs, not fingers.
items.markingKey: (a) sodium [1]; outer electron further / lost more easily [1] [2] (b) any two [1] each [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Ionic bonding usually happens between … (b) Atoms react to form bonds in order to …
items.answer: (a) a metal and a non-metal (b) obtain a full outer shell of electrons
items.markingKey: (a) Metals lose electrons; non-metals gain them. (b) A full outer shell (like a noble gas) is stable.

items.stem: Explain why the formula of magnesium chloride is MgCl₂.
items.answer: Magnesium loses two electrons (Mg²⁺) but each chlorine atom can gain only one (Cl⁻), so two chloride ions are needed to balance the charge.
items.markingKey: Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ [1]; two Cl⁻ balance 2+ [1] [2]

items.stem: Potassium (atomic number 19) reacts with oxygen (atomic number 8) to form potassium oxide. State how many electrons each metal atom loses and give the charges on the two ions.
items.answer: 1 electron lost; K⁺ and O²⁻
items.markingKey: 1 lost [1]; ions K⁺ and O²⁻ [1] [2]

items.stem: Oxygen (atomic number 8) forms a covalent compound with hydrogen. State the number of electrons in the outer shell of an oxygen atom and deduce the formula of the compound.
items.answer: 6 outer electrons; OH₂
items.markingKey: 6 [1]; OH₂ (2 shared pairs) [1] [2]

items.stem: Chlorine (atomic number 17) forms a covalent compound with hydrogen. (a) Give the electron arrangement of chlorine. (b) Explain how many hydrogen atoms bond to each chlorine atom. (c) Name the compound and give its formula.
items.answer: (a) 2,8,7 (b) 1: it needs 1 more electrons for a full outer shell and shares one pair with each hydrogen (c) hydrogen chloride, ClH
items.markingKey: (a) 2,8,7 [1] (b) 1 with reason [1] (c) name and formula [1] [3]

items.stem: Element X has atomic number 20, element Y has atomic number 16 and element Z has atomic number 17. (a) Give the electron arrangement of each element. (b) Predict the type of bond formed between Z and hydrogen and the number of hydrogen atoms that bond to one Z atom. (c) Explain why neither X nor Y forms a bond with argon.
items.answer: (a) X 2,8,8,2; Y 2,8,6; Z 2,8,7 (b) Covalent; 1 hydrogen atom. (c) Argon has a full outer shell (2,8,8), so it does not gain, lose or share electrons.
items.markingKey: (a) all three correct [2]; two correct [1] [2] (b) covalent [1]; 1 [1] [2] (c) full outer shell [1]; no electron transfer or sharing [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why water boils at a much lower temperature than sand (silicon dioxide). (b) Explain why iodine turns to a gas at a low temperature even though the atoms in an iodine molecule are joined by a covalent bond.
items.answer: (a) Water is simple molecular with weak forces between molecules; sand is giant covalent, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken. (b) Only the weak forces between I₂ molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break.
items.markingKey: (a) water weak forces between molecules [1]; sand giant covalent strong bonds [1] [2] (b) weak forces between molecules overcome [1]; covalent bond not broken [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun says: "Salt conducts electricity because it contains metal atoms." Explain why Arjun is wrong.
items.answer: Salt contains ions, and conducts only when molten or dissolved because the ions can then move; solid salt does not conduct.
items.markingKey: ions must move [1]; only molten or dissolved [1] [2]

items.stem: Grace tests three unknown substances. P: melting point 996 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; Q: melting point 1710 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; R: melting point −78 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no. Identify the structure of substance Q and give a reason.
items.answer: Giant covalent: very high melting point and does not conduct even when molten.
items.markingKey: giant covalent [1]; reason from data [1] [2]

items.stem: Chloe reads that graphite is used for a lubricant in machinery, while diamond is used for the tips of drill bits. (a) Explain why graphite is suitable for a lubricant in machinery. (b) Suggest one property, other than melting point, that should be tested before choosing a material.
items.answer: (a) Its layers slide easily. (b) Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches.
items.markingKey: (a) property [1]; linked to structure [1] [2] (b) valid property with reason [1]; Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches [1] [2]
